intro: A hand, an eye or a group of figures can carry a public message. Notice how much of that message depends on the image and how much depends on knowing its setting.
alt: Four examples of political print styles with a painted eye, an open hand, a black-and-cream march and a brightly colored group.

variants.name: Polish Poster School
variants.look: The eye and folded paper combine into one compact, ambiguous image with a brushy edge.
variants.history: Postwar Polish poster artists developed inventive approaches to film, theater and cultural promotion, often using visual metaphor and expressive drawing.
variants.when: Study it when you need a design that hints at a story without illustrating the whole story.
variants.why: A surprising pairing rewards the first glance and gives a viewer something to puzzle over.

variants.name: May '68 poster
variants.look: The open hand reads as a single rough-edged shape in sharply contrasting ink.
variants.history: Print workshops such as the Atelier Populaire produced quickly circulated posters during the May 1968 protests and general strike in France.
variants.when: Study how a mark can be direct enough to read immediately and simple enough to reproduce quickly.
variants.why: An active shape and spare colors make a design work across many copies and viewing conditions.

variants.name: Taller de Gráfica Popular
variants.look: Black shapes and rough cut marks bring people and their movement forward in relief-print contrast.
variants.history: Taller de Gráfica Popular began in Mexico City in 1937. Its members made prints for broad audiences and engaged with social and political life.
variants.when: Study how an inexpensive edition can sustain visible texture and clearly organized figures.
variants.why: Cut highlights make a high-contrast black ink image lively without asking for a second color.

variants.name: AfriCOBRA
variants.look: Luminous color moves around interlocking figures, making the group read as a shared composition.
variants.history: Founded in Chicago in 1968, AfriCOBRA artists combined images, color and often lettering in work made for and about Black communities.
variants.when: Study the members' attributed works for the relationship between repeated bright colors and a broad public audience.
variants.why: Related vivid hues keep individual shapes distinct while binding the whole group into a rhythm.

source.label: Museum of Contemporary Art North Miami

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. As specified, she is the subject of each individual artwork's idiom, or a visitor for works that do not depict people. Style distinctions are immediately clear. Scene list in exact order: Polish Poster School painted graphic featuring an eye emerging from folded paper, expressive brushy symbolic economy, no text; May 1968 poster conventions featuring a single black raised open hand in scratchy vital red/black screenprint, no text; Taller de Gráfica Popular technique study broad-cut black and cream relief print with several people stepping together, modern visitor observes; AfriCOBRA graphic study of confident modern group in luminous rhythmic citrus color, densely interlocked decorative shapes, no legible text and no artist-copy. Modern woman visible beside each original study. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
